title: Listening for the ripe
hookLine: the Anand invites us to hear what is true beneath the noise

lines: A LOUD HALL. SOMEONE SAYS YOUR NAME.
THE EAR PULLS ONE VOICE FROM A ROAR.
WHAT IS YOUR EAR TUNED FOR?
cards: A wedding hall, ten minutes before the food. Two hundred people talking at once, a toddler shrieking, someone testing a microphone. And across the room, through all of it, somebody says your name, and your head turns.

Psychologists call it the cocktail party effect: the ear can pull one voice out of a roar when it's tuned for it. Yesterday the Anand said the hearers of unripe words are unripe too. So what is the ear tuned for?

teach.h: PAURI 24: THE HEARERS CAN BE UNRIPE TOO.
teach.b: Pauri twenty-four, in paraphrase: unripe are those who speak, unripe are those who hear. Guru Amar Das doesn't let the listener off the hook.
A ripe word can fall on an ear that's somewhere else, and then it's as if it was never said. But the Sikh answer isn't to listen less. It's to listen better.

teach.h: IN THE GURDWARA, HEARING IS THE MAIN ACT.
teach.b: Look at a gurdwara. The ragis sing the kirtan, and the sangat listens. The Guru Granth Sahib is read aloud, and the room listens.

Each day a hukamnama, the order, is read from wherever the Guru Granth Sahib opens, and Sikhs hear it as guidance for that day. Hearing sits near the center of it all. Guru Nanak had already said this in the Japji.
Four pauris in a row, eight through eleven, keep beginning their lines with one word, suniai: by listening.

teach.h: TUNE THE EAR LIKE IT'S TUNED FOR YOUR NAME.
teach.b: By listening, they say in paraphrase, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away; by listening, even an ordinary person comes to know truth and contentment. So the Anand's warning and the Japji's praise fit together.
The ear can be unripe, full of the noise of maya, gossip, the scroll.
Or it can be tuned, the way it's tuned for your name in a crowded hall, so that one true sentence comes through.

how: In the gurdwara the sangat largely listens: to kirtan, to the reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and to the day's hukamnama, which Sikhs hear as guidance for that day.

o: by listening, the ear tuned to truth
by reading the scripture in silence
by singing, the voice raised in praise

p: the hearers can be unripe too

s: in the gurdwara, the hukamnama is chosen ahead of time from a list
it's read from wherever the Guru Granth Sahib opens that day.
the Japji has four pauris built on the word suniai
pauris eight to eleven: by listening.
the Anand says only speakers can be unripe
pauri 24 names the hearers as well.

games.q: in the morning the Guru Granth Sahib is opened and a passage is read aloud. what do the listeners take it as?
o: a fortune that predicts their day.
the hukamnama: the day's order, guidance to hear.
a test of how well they know the text.
games.why: it's called the hukamnama, the order, and Sikhs hear it as guidance for that day.

practice: Close your eyes and let the sounds come in, traffic, a fridge, a voice in another room, your own breath, without naming or chasing them.

Then, inside all that, listen for one thing that's simply true right now: my breath is moving, the light is on, someone I love is alive. If you pray, you can listen to Waheguru said once, silently, inside.

wordCard.voice: Suniai, by listening. The Anand warns that hearers can be unripe; the Japji says that by suniai, sorrow is wiped away. Tune the ear for what is true.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: suniai, by listening; the word that opens line after line in Japji pauris 8–11.

carryVoice: Your line: hear the true. The ear that finds your name in a crowd can find that too. Until tomorrow, then.
